claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a single high-temperature BCC phase.
Transformation of high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the Gibbs-free-energy difference between BCC and competing equilibrium phases.
Cooling-rate-dependent kinetic pathways determine the fractions and identities of phases produced during cooling.
The composition of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 makes BCC thermodynamically unstable below a critical temperature.
Lower-temperature transformation occurs through diffusional nucleation and growth mediated by atomic mobility and local composition fluctuations.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for thermodynamically favored phases to nucleate and grow.
Rapid cooling kinetically arrests transformation and preserves a metastable, predominantly BCC microstructure.
Possible lower-temperature products in this alloy include FCC, ordered intermetallic, or sigma phases.
Slow-cooled samples will have larger fractions and sizes of equilibrium phases than rapidly quenched samples.
Integrated simulation and experiment can correlate predicted transformation kinetics with observed microstructural transitions.
A moderate cooling rate produces a known, partially transformed reference microstructure in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The controlled comparison will contrast rapidly quenched and slowly cooled samples of the same composition.
The proposed mechanism applies only when atomic diffusion can occur on the transformation timescale.
Cooling conditions that completely suppress diffusion fall outside the proposed mechanistic domain.
Temperatures at which the interphase free-energy difference is negligible fall outside the proposed mechanistic domain.
Minor elements or impurities may alter diffusion pathways and transformation rates.
A Gibbs-free-energy difference between BCC and FCC can be a critical parameter for an FCC-to-BCC martensitic transformation in metastable multicomponent alloys.
Dual-phase compositionally complex alloys can be sensitive to thermal gradients and solidification conditions.
Failure of slow cooling to increase the equilibrium-phase fraction relative to quenching would falsify the hypothesis.
